blocks.title: 1. Fundamental Definition of Ohm's Law
blocks.content: At constant temperature, the electric current flowing through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across its terminals.

blocks.title: Mathematical Expression of Ohm's Law
blocks.content:
Where:
• V is Electric Potential Difference (measured in Volts, V)
• I is Electric Current (measured in Amperes, A)
• R is Resistance of the conductor (measured in Ohms, Ω)

blocks.title: Crucial Physics Caveat: The Ohmic Condition
blocks.content: Ohm's law is NOT a universal law of nature like Newton's laws. It holds true only when temperature, mechanical strain, and physical state of the conductor remain strictly constant. Non-ohmic devices include diodes, LEDs, and vacuum tubes.

blocks.title: 2. Factors Governing Electrical Resistance
blocks.content:
Experiments show that resistance R of a uniform conductor is:
1. Directly proportional to its length (L)
2. Inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area (A)
3. Dependent on the nature of the material (Resistivity, ρ)
4. Dependent on the temperature (generally increases linearly for pure metals).

blocks.title: Formula for Specific Electrical Resistivity
blocks.content: Resistivity (ρ) is an intrinsic material property. Silver has the lowest resistivity (1.60 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m), making it the finest conductor, while Nichrome has very high resistivity (1.10 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m), making it ideal for heating coils.

blocks.title: 1. Resistors in Series Combination
blocks.content: When two or more resistors are joined end-to-end, they are said to be connected in series. In a series circuit, current (I) remains identical through each resistor, while total potential difference (V) divides across them.

blocks.title: Equivalent Series Resistance Law
blocks.content:
Total potential difference is the algebraic sum of individual voltage drops:
V = V₁ + V₂ + V₃ = I·R₁ + I·R₂ + I·R₃ = I(R₁ + R₂ + R₃)

blocks.title: 2. Resistors in Parallel Combination
blocks.content: When resistors are connected across two common electrical nodes, they are in parallel. In a parallel circuit, potential difference (V) across each resistor is identical, while current (I) divides inversely with resistance.

blocks.title: Equivalent Parallel Resistance Law
blocks.content: The reciprocal of equivalent resistance is the sum of reciprocals of individual resistances. Equivalent resistance is always LESS than the smallest individual resistance in the combination.

les_joule_heating.lessonTitle: Lesson 1.3: Heating Effects of Electric Current & Joule's Law

blocks.title: 1. Mechanism of Electric Heating
blocks.content: When an electric current passes through a conductor with finite resistance, free electrons collide with lattice ions, converting kinetic energy into thermal heat energy.

blocks.title: Joule's Law of Heating Formulation
blocks.formulaLatex: H = I^2 \cdot R \cdot t = V \cdot I \cdot t = \frac{V^2}{R} \cdot t \quad [\text{Joules}]
blocks.content:
Heat produced in a resistor is directly proportional to:
1. Square of electric current (I²)
2. Electrical resistance (R)
3. Time duration of current flow (t)

blocks.title: 2. Electric Power & Commercial Units
blocks.formulaLatex: P = V \cdot I = I^2 \cdot R = \frac{V^2}{R} \quad [\text{Watts}], \quad 1\text{ kWh} = 3.6 \times 10^6 \text{ J}
blocks.content: One kilowatt-hour (1 kWh), commonly called a 'Board of Trade Unit', represents the energy consumed by a 1000W appliance in 1 hour.

blocks.title: 1. Discovery of Electromagnetism by Hans Christian Oersted (1820)
blocks.content: Oersted placed a magnetic compass needle parallel and adjacent to a current-carrying wire. The deflection of the needle proved that moving charges create a surrounding magnetic field.

blocks.title: Maxwell's Right-Hand Thumb Rule
blocks.content: Imagine grasping the conductor in your right hand with thumb pointing in direction of current flow. The curled fingers encircle the wire in the direction of magnetic field lines.

les_lorentz.lessonTitle: Lesson 2.2: Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor

blocks.title: 1. Fleming's Left-Hand Rule for Motors
blocks.content: Stretch the thumb, forefinger, and central finger of your left hand mutually perpendicular. Forefinger = Field (B), Center finger = Current (I), Thumb = Force/Motion (F).

blocks.title: 2. Lorentz Force Formulation
blocks.content: Force is maximum when conductor is perpendicular to field (θ = 90°) and vanishes when parallel (θ = 0°). This torque powers direct-current electric motors.

blocks.title: 1. Faraday's Discovery of Induced Current (1831)
blocks.content: Whenever magnetic flux linked with a closed circuit changes with time, an electromotive force (EMF) is induced, driving an electric current through the circuit.

blocks.title: 2. Faraday's Law & Lenz's Law of Induction
blocks.content: The negative sign (Lenz's Law) states that induced EMF always acts to oppose the change in magnetic flux that produced it, preserving conservation of energy.

les_snell_refraction.lessonTitle: Lesson 3.2: Refraction of Light & Snell's Law

blocks.title: 1. Laws of Optical Refraction
blocks.content: When light travels obliquely across an interface separating two transparent media of different optical densities, its propagation velocity changes, causing the ray to bend.

blocks.title: Snell's Mathematical Law
blocks.content: Where i is angle of incidence, r is angle of refraction, n₁ and n₂ are absolute refractive indices, and v₁, v₂ are phase velocities in the respective media.

blocks.title: 2. Total Internal Reflection & Critical Angle
blocks.content: When light travels from an optically denser medium to a rarer medium at an angle exceeding critical angle (i > i_c), 100% of light energy is reflected internally. This powers fiber optics and endoscopes.

blocks.title: 1. Ray Tracing in Thin Convex and Concave Lenses
blocks.content: A lens is a transparent optical material bounded by two refracting surfaces. Convex lenses are converging (positive focal length), while concave lenses are diverging (negative focal length).

blocks.title: 2. Thin Lens Equation & Optical Power
blocks.content: Optical power measures the degree of convergence or divergence. A lens with focal length f = +0.5 m has a power of +2.0 D (hypermetropia correction).
